alternatives: Levetiracetam: renally cleared, no cytochrome P450 interaction with carbamazepine, sertraline, levothyroxine or macrolides
Azithromycin: minimal CYP3A4 inhibition; no clinically significant carbamazepine interaction
output.formulary_status: Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and lacosamide IV, azithromycin, amoxicillin and doxycycline: formulary.
interactions: Clarithromycin + carbamazepine: clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, the main route of carbamazepine metabolism; carbamazepine concentrations rise, with ataxia, diplopia, sedation, cardiac conduction delay and, at high levels, seizures; avoid the combination
Erythromycin or fluconazole + carbamazepine: CYP3A4 inhibition; same effect; avoid
Doxycycline + carbamazepine: carbamazepine induces doxycycline metabolism and shortens its half-life; reduced antibiotic exposure
Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): no CYP3A4 interaction, but they lower the seizure threshold; avoid in a patient with seizures
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + carbamazepine: additive sodium-channel blockade and conduction effects; complex two-way enzyme interaction; avoid with carbamazepine toxicity
Lacosamide + carbamazepine: additive sodium-channel effect and PR prolongation; avoid with first-degree AV block
Carbamazepine + sertraline: carbamazepine induces sertraline metabolism and lowers its concentration
Carbamazepine + levothyroxine: carbamazepine increases levothyroxine clearance; monitor TSH
output.proposed: Clarithromycin and antiseizure options (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, lacosamide, valproate) against current carbamazepine, sertraline and levothyroxine
output.summary: Clarithromycin inhibits carbamazepine metabolism through CYP3A4. Fosphenytoin and lacosamide add sodium-channel and conduction effects to carbamazepine. Valproate is listed as an allergy. Levetiracetam has no interaction. Fluoroquinolones lower the seizure threshold.
warnings: Carbamazepine at supratherapeutic concentrations: monitor ECG for PR and QRS prolongation
Lorazepam: no pharmacokinetic interaction; monitor respiration and blood pressure

output.query: Carbamazepine clarithromycin interaction and status epilepticus treatment

results.finding: Clarithromycin and erythromycin inhibit CYP3A4 and raise carbamazepine concentrations; azithromycin has little CYP3A4 effect.
Supratherapeutic carbamazepine concentrations can paradoxically provoke seizures and slow cardiac conduction.
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine [Glauser_2016].
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective as second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019].

output.summary: Macrolides other than azithromycin raise carbamazepine levels through CYP3A4 inhibition, and high carbamazepine levels can provoke seizures. Status epilepticus is treated with a benzodiazepine and then one of three equally effective second-line drugs [Glauser_2016; ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, carbamazepine level
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the carbamazepine level shows whether the clarithromycin course has made it toxic [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: The clarithromycin-carbamazepine interaction is the mechanism of the toxicity, and the antibiotic and the second-line ASM must be chosen against carbamazepine and the valproate allergy [ESETT_2019].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue clarithromycin with carbamazepine: the interaction is the cause.
Do not load fosphenytoin or phenytoin, or lacosamide, with toxic carbamazepine and first-degree AV block.
Do not use valproate: documented thrombocytopenia and pancreatitis.
Do not switch to a fluoroquinolone for the pneumonia: fluoroquinolones lower the seizure threshold.
Do not use other CYP3A4 inhibitors (for example erythromycin or fluconazole) with carbamazepine.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid valproate because of the documented thrombocytopenia and pancreatitis, and fosphenytoin or lacosamide because they add sodium-channel and conduction effects to toxic carbamazepine with first-degree AV block [ESETT_2019].
Hold carbamazepine and repeat the level in 12 to 24 hours; restart at a level-guided dose once it is back in range.
Stop clarithromycin and complete the pneumonia treatment with a non-interacting antibiotic that does not lower the seizure threshold (for example amoxicillin or azithromycin).
Continuous cardiac monitoring while the carbamazepine level falls (first-degree AV block).
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
An ambulatory Holter adds nothing: the conduction delay is on the 12-lead ECG, and inpatient telemetry while the carbamazepine level falls is part of management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Status epilepticus from carbamazepine toxicity due to CYP3A4 inhibition by clarithromycin in left temporal focal epilepsy

key_clinical_evidence: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; with carbamazepine (a CYP3A4 substrate) it raises carbamazepine into the toxic range
Carbamazepine toxicity slows cardiac conduction (first-degree AV block here) and can provoke seizures
Azithromycin or amoxicillin avoids the interaction; fluoroquinolones lower the seizure threshold
Of the ESETT second-line drugs only levetiracetam suits here: valproate allergy and sodium-channel toxicity

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Clarke is a 52-year-old man with left temporal focal epilepsy on carbamazepine who is brought by ambulance after his wife called 911 when he developed a focal seizure with impaired awareness, lip smacking and left hand automatisms, followed by right arm dystonic posturing and right-sided clonic jerking, which spread to bilateral tonic-clonic activity after 2 minutes. The seizure has been continuous for 15 minutes. He took his medications yesterday but his wife is not sure about his compliance over the past week as he has been working very long hours with minimal sleep. He started a new 10-day antibiotic course 4 days ago for community-acquired pneumonia: he was prescribed clarithromycin by his primary care physician. For the past 2 days he has complained of dizziness, unsteadiness and double vision. He has a documented valproate allergy (thrombocytopenia and pancreatitis). His hypothyroidism is stable on levothyroxine.
